note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting for a diabetes review following a hypoglycaemic episode.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred last Tuesday after skipping lunch while gardening.
The patient experienced symptoms including sweating, shakiness, and inability to think straight during the episode.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused.
The patient's daughter measured capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L.
The patient recovered within 15 minutes after treatment.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient does not have neuropathic symptoms.
The patient has no visual problems.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1 gram twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 milligrams.
The patient is prescribed Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
Pedal pulses are palpable.
Monofilament sensation is normal in both feet.
There is a callus under the ball of the left first metatarsal head.
The patient's blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kilos.
The patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is up from 58.
The patient's eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The impression is Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide.
The patient has stable CKD stage 3a.
The patient has a low-risk foot with a callus.
The plan is to reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only.
The plan is to start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
The plan includes providing a leaflet on sick day rules.
The plan includes a referral to the podiatrist for the callus.
The plan includes booking a retinal screening.
The plan is to review the patient in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.
Safety netting includes checking blood glucose before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
Safety netting includes not driving if blood sugar is below 5 mmol/L.
Safety netting includes keeping fast-acting glucose in the car.
Safety netting includes stopping driving and informing the DVLA if there is another severe hypo within 12 months or any hypo while driving.
Safety netting includes stopping empagliflozin use if the patient is vomiting, has diarrhoea, or is unable to eat and drink.

transcript_facts.fact: The patient experienced symptoms including being all sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The patient states the episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and they had just put them out.
The patient states they had been in the garden all morning and skipped their lunch.
The relative found the patient confused and noted they have type 1 diabetes themselves.
The relative treated the patient with orange juice and biscuits.
The relative states the patient was back to normal after about fifteen minutes.
The relative used their meter and the capillary glucose reading was 2.8.
The patient states they sometimes feel a bit wobbly before tea.
The patient states they drive to the shops and to their allotment.
The clinician asks about the patient's medicines, specifically Metformin 1 gram twice a day.
The patient confirms they are on Metformin 1 gram twice a day.
The clinician asks about Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day.
The patient confirms they take Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day, specifically in the morning and at teatime.
The clinician asks about Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The patient confirms they take Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The clinician asks about allergies.
The patient states they have no known drug allergies.
The clinician asks about problems with feet, tingling, or numbness.
The patient states their feet have been fine.
The relative states they have pins and needles in their hands at night, which they reckon is carpal tunnel.
The clinician suggests sticking with the patient's dad today and asks about eyesight problems.
The patient states they have no problems with their eyesight and their eye screening is due.
The clinician reports the patient's blood tests from last week: HbA1c is 62, up from 58 last time.
The clinician reports the patient's kidney function (eGFR) is 52, which is about the same as before.
The patient asks if the results are bad.
The clinician notes that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypo worries them more.
The clinician checks the patient's feet and notes that pulses are fine in both feet.
The clinician notes there is a bit of hard skin, a callus, under the ball of the left foot, by the big toe.
The patient states they have had the callus for ages.
The clinician notes the patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84 and their weight is 91 kilos.
The clinician suggests reducing the gliclazide dose to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
The clinician suggests adding empagliflozin 10 milligrams once a day.
The clinician advises stopping empagliflozin when unwell and not eating or drinking (e.g., with vomiting or diarrhoea) until better.
The clinician advises checking blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The clinician advises not driving if blood sugar is below five.
The clinician advises keeping some sugary snacks in the car.
The clinician advises that needing daughter's help counts as a severe hypo.
The clinician advises that if there is another severe hypo within 12 months, or any hypo while driving, the patient must stop driving and tell the DVLA.
The relative offers to get the patient some glucose tablets.
The clinician refers the patient to the podiatrist for the callus and advises booking the eye screening.
The clinician states they will see the patient in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.
